elaborate: Ted Nelson's stretchtext, from his Hypertext Note 8 of 1967, renamed so the wider business can see what it means

ground.quote: In 1967 Ted Nelson described stretchtext: text that "stretches, becoming longer, with replacement phrases, new details and additional clauses popping into place", and shrinks back on demand, while "the reader remains oriented" (Hypertext Note 8).
In 1970 he put it like this: "Gaps appear between phrases; new words and phrases pop into the gaps, an item at a time."

ground.quote: Elastic documents never spread because an author had to write every level by hand. An LLM can now produce the levels. The open question is fidelity: whether the reader can always tell what the author said from what the AI added.

derive: An author had to write every level of detail by hand.
Writing every level costs more than most documents can bear.
So stretchtext stayed a demonstration rather than a way of writing.
challenge: LLMs shorten text well and expand it poorly, and expansion invites invention (Jensenius 2025).

elaborate: not specific to software: a bid, a contract, a policy or a board paper serves readers who need different depths.
A director wants the conclusion; a reviewer needs the clause behind it

ground.quote: For example, "three teams report the same approval bottleneck" opens into the three excerpts, their dates and how they differ. A client could then trust the analysis, and argue with it, without rereading every transcript.
